parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the direction of the magnetic field in Fig. 9.1 and ask yourself which side of the slice lies along that same direction - $t$ is the thickness measured parallel to $B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify What $t$ Means**
In the Hall formula $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ the distance $t$ is the thickness of the conductor measured in the same direction as the magnetic field $B$. It is the separation between the two faces that the field enters and leaves.

Step 2: **Read The Geometry From The Diagram**
Here $B$ is vertical, normal to face QRYZ, in the direction from Q to P. The only side of the slice that is vertical is the $0.10\text{ mm}$ side marked XY. So $$t = 0.10\text{ mm}$$

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: unit conversion from mm to m
hints: Hint 1: List all the values you need for $B$, $I$, $n$ and $t$, and check their SI units carefully - the thickness from (a) must be in metres, and the charge $q$ on each free electron is the elementary charge $e$.
Hint 2: Substitute the values into $V_H = BI/ntq$ with $t = 0.10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$, then evaluate to 2 significant figures with the unit volt.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Collect The Data In SI Units**
You are sitting with the formula and the data side by side. The physics is already done for you, you just need consistent units. $$B = 0.13\text{ T}, \quad I = 3.8\text{ A}$$ $$n = 6.0 \times 10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}, \quad q = e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$$ $$t = 0.10\text{ mm} = 0.10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}$$ A very common slip is to leave $t$ in mm, which makes the answer 1000 times too large.

Step 2: **Substitute Into The Hall Expression**
Now put everything into the given expression: $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq} = \frac{0.13 \times 3.8}{(6.0 \times 10^{28})(1.0 \times 10^{-4})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}$$ Numerator: $0.13 \times 3.8 = 0.494$. Denominator: $6.0 \times 10^{28} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 9.6 \times 10^{5}$.

Step 3: **Calculate The Magnitude**
$$V_H = \frac{0.494}{9.6 \times 10^{5}} \approx 5.1 \times 10^{-7}\text{ V}$$ This tiny sub-microvolt value is typical for a metal Hall probe because $n$ is so large.
